Learning Resources Botley The Coding Robot - 45 Pieces, Ages 5+ Screen- Free Coding Toys, Coding STEM Toy for Kids, Coding for Kids,Back to School Gifts,Teacher Supplies Botley is quite a versatile fellow.

My four year old is having fun running him around in "line" mode, where his sensors follow a black lined path on a white background. When he reaches the end, he turns around and comes back.

Daddy is having a little more fun with "code" mode, which is too complex for the little one at this point. You program multiple commands into the remote, and then you send Botley out on a small adventure, around the obstacle course pieces that you can set up with material from the box. It's simple and easy for an adult, but for kids, it will teach computer programming basics, planning ahead, and thinking before you act.

The box comes with a variety of cones, bricks and blocks, as well as arms for Botley and cards that can help you measure how far he's going to move, and doubles as a wavy black line pattern on the reverse side if you want to use it. All told, it's a fun and complete package, although I wish the instructions were a little more explicit for adults, and a little more fun for little ones to explore on their own. As it stands, the manual explains a few little tasks you can try, written in tiny font in as few pages as humanly possible. I want more from this.
text_fidelity_b: Learning Resources Botley The Coding Robot - 45 Pieces, Ages 5+ Screen- Free Coding Toys, Coding STEM Toy for Kids, Coding for Kids,Back to School Gifts,Teacher Supplies

The presentation is nice: the box is nice, thick, and has a slide to it - a drawer. There is a little strap/ribbon to pull it open. It does feel “different,” nicer if you will. Having only begun we’re still getting used to it, but it’s not so different you can’t do it. Actually - without trying - we were thinking it makes bending the pieces harder.

There is a sort of “dust” that it leaves behind. I pulled out the bag onto a small table and when returning to the drawer this dust was left on the table - something like a sawdust, but not. Just a heads up - it was easy to clean.

This is a great puzzle and we liked this one so much we got a second one. This will be nice for some great time chilling with my wife. Happy to recommend.

Rockin' Rider Legacy Grow-with-Me Pony, Large Anyone who remembers the old TV series "The Lone Ranger" will recognize the title of this review. I give you my condolences because, like me, you are older than dirt.

My wife and I saw this Rockin' Rider Legacy Grow-with-Me Pony at our young nephew's second birthday party. It looked very sturdy, was colorful and well-built, and the children were lining up to give it a try. Since we had our granddaughter's second birthday coming up we decided to order one for her.

Safety is of course a big concern when buying something for any young child. However this particular rocking horse is well stabilized and provides extra protection as far as balance. Of course children can fall down at a moment's notice and for any number of reasons so it makes sense to always watch your child in whatever activity they're involved in.

Safer than the original rocking horse designs, painted with vivid colors, and having a very low center of gravity -- and thus superior balance and stability -- this Rockin' Rider keeps our granddaughter entertained daily, at least until she tires of it and moves on looking for other things to get into. Highly recommended as the safest rocking horse we've seen.
text_fidelity_b: Rockin' Rider Legacy Grow-with-Me Pony, Large

My 22 month old son loves this toy. He loves the songs (he regularly dances to them), the ability to put coins in the bank and that there are two of each color for sorting. I would highly recommend this toy for 7 months to 2 1/2 years but would suggest purchasing in a brick and mortar store to verify the door closes properly (or be open to contacting customer service if you have the same issue).

text_fidelity_a: Doggie Doo Corgi Game - Unpredictable Action - Feed The Doggie and Collect His Doo to Win - Includes 24-Piece Puzzle by Goliath This type of thing isn't usually my cup of tea and I typically dislike potty humor. This looked like something to bring humor on the days that my guys aren't getting along, though. It is on the weird side(even thought so from my 3 boys), with all the noises, but it is also on the humorous side. To play, you stick a bit of slime("food") into the bone. The players take turns rolling the die and squeezing the bone the amount rolled. Each player has a shovel that they place behind the dog to catch the "doos" before squeezing the bone. Each time the dog poos, you have to refill the bone. Once all the slime is gone, the player with the most "doos" wins. Had I known that the game used slime, I never would have gotten it. I've had to throw out too many items ruined from it to want it in my home anymore. We just try to be extra careful when playing. It comes with two bags, but it only takes one to play. The second bag is for if the first gets ruined. It says on the bag that it's non-toxic, but to still wash hands after touching it. When the game works, it's fun and makes us laugh. We've had lots of trouble getting it to work properly, though. Many times it won't seal just right(I guess) and no amount of squeezing the bone will make anything happen. It warns not to put too much, which we've tried not to do, and to also make sure the bone is pushed all the way in, which we've tried to do. It still won't work for us half the time, though, which makes it frustrating. If the slime ever gets stuck, the game does come with a stick to push it out. It also comes with a puzzle, which is a nice bonus. Overall, it's still a fun game.
text_fidelity_b: Doggie Doo Corgi Game - Unpredictable Action - Feed The Doggie and Collect His Doo to Win - Includes 24-Piece Puzzle by Goliath

Cherry-O Board Game for 2 to 4 Players Kids Ages 3 and Up (Amazon Exclusive) You really can't go wrong with this game if you've got little ones around(unless, of course, they put things other than food in their mouth, and then I'd save this for later). My husband has fond memories of playing this game with his grandmother, but about a month ago was the first time I'd ever played it. My children have fallen in love with the game, and I'm thrilled they've had the chance to experience it. It's cute and fun!

It's a really quick and simple game to play, and easy enough for very young players to be included, since counting only goes to 4 in the game. (Again, the fruit is very small, though, so don't have it around those that put things in their mouths.) It's actually just right for my 3 year old, and while it's technically too easy for my 5 and 8 year old children, they still love playing it.

Also, with small pieces, I appreciate that there are 4 extra pieces of fruit(one of each color) included in case one goes missing.

Overall, this is a perfect game for preschoolers to play, as long as they don't put things in their mouth.

HobbyZone Champ RTF, HBZ4900 This is a great little plane, no question. But I ignored Hobbyzone's recommendation for 14 years old and up. I bought two: one for each of my 9-year-old twin sons, who were hot to fly RC model airplanes. One learned to fly quickly, but the other has been seriously disappointed. And I had to learn quickly how to use styrofoam glue to reattach broken wings, tail parts, motor mounts, etc.

It took me a while to understand how critical the trim really is: a beginner really can't fly a plane that isn't trimmed properly. You can get the trim in the ballpark with visual inspection of the control surfaces, but to get it right you have to fly the plane yourself. When I did that, and touched up the trim, flying became a lot of fun - for one boy. The other boy still can't fly more than a few seconds before landing his plane on its nose. He has just about given up in disgust.

I suspect that in a year or two both boys will have good flying skills. But in the meantime one boy is ready to move up while the other is ready to give up. Bummer!
text_fidelity_b: HobbyZone Champ RTF, HBZ4900

text_fidelity_a:
T.S. Shure Wooden Magnetic World Map Puzzle [[VIDEOID:86f83f42426788872f7319ab9d100512]]I loved this world map. It's big and solid. It's bright and colorful. It was fun to play with and put together. It had really informational highlights about each country, such as eskimos and igloos in Greenland.

This came packaged extremely well. I was very surprised that the edges weren't bent at all after I opened it, and this was because of the high quality packaging. The packaging from T.S. Sure had multiple layers of cardboard surrounding this puzzle, and then it was all contained inside of a nice big amazon box. So, there was no chance of this getting damaged during shipment. And, that was a possibility. This is pretty heavy, about ten pounds. And, it has a high quality wood backing. It looks very nice, back and front.

I liked the projection that they based the map on. For example, Greenland is realistically much smaller than Africa. The only negative is that the magnets aren't very sticky.

I'd highly recommend it for every classroom. I'd also recommend it for your home, too. It's beautiful and educational.

Pros:
+Very solid
+Great world map, that shows Africa as its true size in comparison to the US
+Or in other words, doesn't use the Mercator Projection
+Has very informative information about each country
+You can stick the magnets to your fridge, too
+Extremely excellent packaging
+Very high quality wood backing

Cons:
-The magnets aren't very strong, so you'll be rearranging them a lot
text_fidelity_b: T.S. Shure Wooden Magnetic World Map Puzzle

Ticket to Ride Rails & Sails Board Game | Train Route-Building Strategy Game | Fun Family Game for Kids and Adults | Ages 10+ | 2-5 Players | Average Playtime 90-120 Minutes | Made by Days of Wonder This version adds difficulty without making it more interesting. In this game, there are both railways and ship routes to build, which means you have to collect cards for each route in the correct color and mode of transportation. Effectively, this game adds twice the number of colors you have to collect to build things. In the original game, you always end up with a bunch of cards in your hand that aren't useful to you because they're not the colors you need to finish your tickets. This game is twice as bad in that regard. Furthermore, there are fewer ship cards, even though you're expected to build more ship routes than train routes. Many of the ship cards are actually worth 2 of that color, which theoretically allows you to collect fewer cards of that color before building, but what actually happens is that you can go through the entire stack of ship cards without getting what you need because the other players are unintentionally hoarding the few cards in the color and type you need.

I didn't hate this game, but I wouldn't play it again.
text_fidelity_b: Ticket to Ride Rails & Sails Board Game | Train Route-Building Strategy Game | Fun Family Game for Kids and Adults | Ages 10+ | 2-5 Players | Average Playtime 90-120 Minutes | Made by Days of Wonder

text_fidelity_a:
Bicycle Fumbling Ferrets This word game is for 3 – 5 players. It’s for ages 10 and up. Takes 30-minutes to play.

It comes in a cardboard box measuring just under 10” X 6.25” X 2.25”. It’s part of the United States Playing Card company, which makes Bicycle playing cards. Made in China.

Each player receives chips, totaling 30-points, to start. You also receive two cards. From there you go around and each person “pays” for additional cards. Cards with letters which are worth more. . . cost more. You go around four-times. At the end, everyone turns-over their cards and you have thirty-seconds to spell a word with the most points. Please Note: Timer not included. Whomever wins that round gets chips equaling the number of points for their winning word. Then the second place person receives chips worth their number and so on. After playing three times, the person with the most points wins.

FYI. . . This came was originally going to be called “The World Series of AlphaBets”. . . but somewhere along the way they changed it to “Fumbling Ferrets”, probably to make it sound more “family friendly”. But it has nothing to do with ferrets.

If you like word / spelling games, then this one is fairly easy and fast to play. If you’re playing with younger kids, especially to start, you may wish to extend the timer to come-up with a word by a little bit and then shorten it with each round.
text_fidelity_b: Bicycle Fumbling Ferrets

It only took a few reminders, but now the dogs are not barking, either inside or when we go out (even if I don't have a squirt gun with me). All I have to do is pick one up and they immediately run off and cower QUIETLY in the bedroom! I think what makes these work better than dog whistles or scolding or time outs is that they can be targeted at the instigator, not both dogs. So if one dog is quiet, he doesn't get shot; just the offender gets blasted. They figured it out really quickly. They do NOT like to be blasted! LOL! And I think they actually compete to see which one can stay the quietest.

Got these to blast the dogs when they won't stop barking. They don't blast a targeted enough stream unless you are standing closer to the dog, like maybe six feet away, but they seem to work for their intended purpose. The chiweenie Bingo's the really rotten one, and the first time I used one of these pistols, I shot him once, he turned around and defiantly barked at me; I shot him again, same thing; then I shot him in the face with it, and he ran off into another room and stopped barking. The first time I used it with Doobie, a Jack Chi, he responded right away. (These dogs hate getting wet...but a dog who loves water would react differently. Still might quit barking, though.) So I'm hopeful these are going to get the job done. Only time will tell, but so far they see the brightly colored gun in my hand and quit barking.

text_fidelity_a:
Venn Board Game | Family Game for 2+ Players | Cooperative & Competitive Gameplay Variations | Creative Word Association Game Featuring Unique Gameplay & Custom Artwork | Ages 10+ Venn is a party game that plays a large number of players, and it comes with a competitive mode and a cooperative mode. The cooperative mode was not fun for our family, so we'll focus on the competitive game. In this game, you use cards with odd artwork to get your teammates to guess a set of three out of twelve possible games. The cards go in one of the seven different sections of a three-way Venn Diagram like you used to see in school. Using the clues you're given, you attempt to identify the three chosen words that the card placer is going for.

There are some fun times to be had here, but a few problems as well. The art is meant to be odd and unusual, but a good amount of it is just plain bad - characters are off-center, objects look like they're floating in the background, etc - and the cards are hard to use because they don't actually fit inside the sections of the Venn diagram. The words are usually very descriptive, but there are also some bad word chocies in the deck like "great" or "interesting" which could literally mean anything.

Unfortunately, this is competing in a crowded market - competitive, team-based family games have been done to death, so if you want to stand out, choose a game like Codenames or Just One or So Clover or...well, there's a lot of them, and they're mostly better than this.
text_fidelity_b: Venn Board Game | Family Game for 2+ Players | Cooperative & Competitive Gameplay Variations | Creative Word Association Game Featuring Unique Gameplay & Custom Artwork | Ages 10+

text_fidelity_a:
Kubros Despicable Me Minion Building Kit We're huge Lego fans in my house, so while it may not be fair, I couldn't help but compare Mega Bloks with Lego. We got a few kits to try out, but otherwise, we've only used Lego in the past(though quite a bit of it). Unfortunately, Mega Bloks has just fallen short, for me, and I wasn't overly impressed.

First of all, I've been spoiled to numbered bags. While this kit is divided into 4 separate bags, you have to open all of them and dump them out, because the pieces you need for each step could be in any of the bags. I prefer, if I'm using a kit, to have my steps divided by bags. It keeps thing from getting less jumbled and lost. It kind of made me wonder what the point of 4 bags were.

Second, these blocks just didn't go together smoothly. Some of them require a great deal of pressure to get attached. They hurt my fingers. I even snapped my finger between two of the blocks at one point trying to get pieces together. (Sad, but true.) My fingers ache after working with Mega Bloks, just because of the pressure I have to use to get them attached.

Third, the directions aren't as clear as I'd prefer. Sure, as an adult, I figured things out, but for the average child, the directions just make things harder than they have to be.

When I discovered that Mega Bloks were compatible with Lego, I was really excited. I thought that the block building world could open up to more options for me and my children. We're sticking with Lego, though! It seems more organized and the pieces are more reliable. (They have more of a perfect fit than we've experienced with Mega Bloks.)

IF you are a fan of Mega Bloks, this kit is cute! (I just found it a pain. Literally. To be fair, though, I probably would have enjoyed the whole experience more, minus the finger pain, if I wasn't so spoiled from better. It really is cute enough!)
text_fidelity_b: Kubros Despicable Me Minion Building Kit

LeapFrog My Pal Violet (Frustration Free Packaging) Three of my four kids have had a LeapFrog My Pal Scout or Violet. Our first born would have had one but I don't think they were made back then. These little interactive toys are so great! Here's why I think your little ones will love them too!

1) It doesn't just talk, Scout/Violet says your child's name, puts their name into songs, and engages the child on a personal level. As soon as my kids realized it was talking to them they would laugh and try to make it do it again. It is still their favorite feature.
2) You can further personalize the Scout/Violet to sing/talk about your child's favorite animal, food and color. The pup uses these favorite things in silly songs. Warning: they are catchy and you will get them stuck in your head!
3) When your child changes, so does Scout/Violet. Anytime the favorites change you can just set the pup to match. The cord to plug it into your computer (USB) is housed right in the back of the pup. Once upon a time the cord was not attached. Be thankful it can't get lost with these newer models.
4) It plays "Bedtime Music" to which you can decide how many minutes it will play. My kids don't sleep to music so we've never used this feature officially, but they still like to press the paw and turn it on and off and on and off and on and off.

I would recommend this to babies 6+ months up to 2 years. My daughter is almost 4 and still plays with hers, but she's really too old for it now.
text_fidelity_b: LeapFrog My Pal Violet (Frustration Free Packaging)

text_fidelity_a:
Paw Patrol Mission Chase Figure (Due to the malfunctions on our particular dog, and the fact that he doesn't walk at all, I was tempted to give it 3 stars, but he's so cute and fun, I went with 4.)

I have a few Paw Patrol fans in my house, so this is a pretty amazing toy.

By pressing the badge on the front of Chase, your children are given a mission. Chase talks and interacts through these missions. For example, chickens have gotten loose, and your child needs to help gather them up. The net compartment opens up, and your child will fire the net out. Chase comments on catching one, and then asks for the net to be reloaded. (One time the net got stuck, and didn't fire out, but he still exclaimed praise at catching a chicken, so it's not perfect.) He won't interact to various things that your child says, but he does have built in interaction, which is still pretty cool.

There are 24 different missions, and Chase moves around a bit through these. I was expecting him to walk a bit, but he never did. He just moves his head around, and moves from crouching to standing positions. There are two compartments on his backpack. One has a net launcher. The other has a microphone(that your child can talk into) and a flashlight. There are various buttons for each feature. (One for opening each compartment, one on the net launcher to launch, one to make the light come on the flashlight, and one to turn on the microphone.) Some of the items come on automatically through missions, but others require your child's assistance, when Chase asks.

Although this is an awesome toy that I'm pretty sure any Paw Patrol fan will love, we did have a couple of negatives with ours.

When the box was first opened, the head was detached a bit, but thankfully, it went back on pretty easily. Also, the button to launch the microphone/flashlight wouldn't work. I tried everything I could to make it work, short of tearing it apart, and tried numerous times, but it never worked. It didn't work when it was supposed to automatically open during missions, either. Thankfully, we can just pull that compartment open. During missions when a child is asked to launch the microphone/flashlight, pulling open the door makes the task recognized, just as if the button worked. So, it's not a huge deal, but still disappointing.

I really do wish he walked a bit, too! The way he's designed, it looked as if he would.

A couple of notes:
-This toy DOES come with batteries, but require 4 AA if you'd like to buy extras.
-If your child can read, know that the box this is delivered in says what's inside, though there are no pictures.
text_fidelity_b: Paw Patrol Mission Chase Figure

LEGO Technic Stunt Show Truck & Bike 42106; Includes Stunt Motorcycle, Toy Truck and Trailer (P10 Pieces) LEGO Technic is very different from regular LEGO blocks, even though they can combine, but the difference is strong enough that this will be a very different type of challenge for young builders. The fact is, this is one of the more simplistic Technic kits we've tried, and that makes this Technic set a good one for those who have never built with this style of blocks before. These are more "Engineer-y" than the standard sets, and will teach simple mechanical principles as you build the pull-motion propulsion system from scratch, and kids can see how it comes together.

If regular LEGO is a teaching toy, this is even better.

That said, Technic is harder to be creative with, so these blocks don't get a lot of play with the standard set once the fun of the kit wears away. My daughter had a little trouble building this, but she is on the younger edge of the age range, so Dad had to do a number of the trickier steps.

I recommend possibly not taking the pieces off of the brackets until they are needed, this way they won't get lost. text_fidelity_a:
Winning Moves Games Sorry Classic Edition Board Game, Multicolor My first introduction to the board game of Sorry was in the early 60's. Sorry was one of the more fast and fun games. The object of the game is to be the first player to move all 4 of your men around the board to get back home. You choose from 4 different colors of your men and your home- blue, green, yellow or red. There is a deck of cards that tell you how many spaces to move your man, and of course it isn't as easy as just moving your man as quickly as you can around the board to get home before anyone and win the game. There are obstacles along the way, should a player get to slide, he slides everyone in his way back to start, and no two men can occupy the same space, so someone has to go back to start- Sorry!

I remember when we played with 2 players, the game took about 15-20 minutes, but with 4 players, it took close to half an hour. It's very fast moving and even faster when hardly any players are sent back to start. I really love the look of this classic 1939 Sorry Game- it's a little different from the one we played on in the 60's. text_fidelity_a:
Forbidden Island – The Cooperative Strategy Survival Island Board Game,2-4 players My wife and I bought this as we are getting more into tabletop gaming (thanks Wil and Felicia!) and I wanted something adventurous and less involved than a city- farm- building simulation game.
This is fairly fun, but the main reason I am writing a review is to specify why I didn't give it four stars and who should get the most enjoyment out of it.
To start out, you choose (randomly for a bit of extra challenge) a character class. These are more realistic classes such as a SCUBA diver, rather than a mage or warrior. Each class has a different special ability, for example the diver can traverse water tiles more easily than other classes. Then you randomly generate the playing field by placing the heavier island cards in a specific formation. Combining the random character roles and the random board is a clever way to make every game different and make sure the players have to think critically rather than relying too much on rote strategies.
Your goal is to traverse the board to collect treasures, cooperating with your fellow players by using each person's ability and the convenience of their position on the board. You may even bail each other out of dire situations by airlifting them to safety or using your special ability, because while you are trying to reach the treasures the island is constantly flooding.
If you ever wanted to play Indiana Jones this is a pretty good start. But for my wife and I to keep it interesting, we have to play on the hardest difficulty level (starting out with more of the island in a flooded state) and even still we have succeeded at our task 100% of the time. Because of this, the game gets old too quickly, which is a shame since the premise is fun, the concept is exciting, the gameplay is perfectly tight, and the artwork is gorgeous.
I do think there is a more appropriate audience for this, which is kids of perhaps 9 years to 13 years playing with other kids or in a mixed group with adults. I think the game will be more challenging for kids and I think playing with kids will make it more fun for the parents/cousins/uncles and aunts etc.
For two adults who are strategy-oriented people, there are more complicated games that are perhaps less beautiful and tightly designed but nonetheless more consistently engaging.
text_fidelity_b: Forbidden Island – The Cooperative Strategy Survival Island Board Game,2-4 players

White Mountain Puzzles The Eighties - 1000 Piece Jigsaw Puzzle [[VIDEOID:b94eac5104dc142a073b662ff11284e3]] I loved this amazing puzzle. The artwork is fantastic! This is a painting of a whole bunch of pictures and other scenes and people from the 1980's. It's based on a painting by Jim Mellet, and his art is amazing! It takes a ton of scenes and people from the 1980's, and turns it into a wonderful painted collage.

The quality of the puzzle is top-notch. The pieces are very thick, and so they fit together well. In my video, you can see that I can actually pick up the entire puzzle, which is usually impossible to do with most puzzles. The backing is a nice blue color, so you can easily tell which pieces are upside down. The border is awesome. The puzzle is surrounded by a red and orange line. This makes the border really easy to put together, and it makes it very easy to identify the edge pieces.

The puzzle is challenging, but it's also very doable. In most puzzles, there's a huge spot of the same color that's very boring, and this puzzle didn't have any of this. I felt entertained and challenged throughout. It's also a great conversation starter, because it has so many iconic people and scenes. I especially liked the Atari, Donkey Kong, Pac-Man, and Mr. T.

Pros:
+Challenging, yet doable
+Fun events and people from the 1980's
+Excellent artwork
+High quality puzzle

Cons:

text_fidelity_a:
BOOMco. Rapid Madness Blaster (Discontinued by manufacturer) I'm just combining my thoughts on the various guns and products into one review, in case anyone would like to do a bit of comparing in one spot.

Darts:

The darts are kind of like a third of a straw, with a cool rubber-like tip. These tips ONLY stick to the special targets, which are on the shields(both the wearable ones and the ones that attach to the guns). There are also targets that stick to the wall. (I just taped the top of these targets, as opposed to sticking the whole thing on the wall.) We tested these out on mirrors and windows. They really don't stick to anything, but the special targets.

They're mostly bright colored, which makes it easier to find them once they've been shot. You'll have to take several time outs just to gather darts.

This company has made it perfectly clear that these darts are NOT made for little ones. I just want to reinforce that. I have an 18 month old that puts things in his mouth constantly. We found a large rock in his poo diaper. :S These are simply irresistible to him with their chewy rubber tip. He's chewed the tops off a few of them, even when we were trying to keep a close eye on him. The tops DO come off when chewed on, so these are definitely a choking hazard for little ones.

I try to teach our boys to never aim a gun at anyone, but I've been hit with a few of the darts. One hurt, but the others didn't. I think it depends on how close the gun is, and simply how the dart hits a person. In general, they don't seem to hurt too much.

Other than chewing, they seem pretty sturdy, though. They're had lots of use and bending, but they still work in the guns.

Farshot Blaster:

This is the smallest gun in this line(that we have...there seems to be a smaller "clipfire"). You pull back the top to "pump it up". It will only hold 1 dart at a time for shooting, but 2 spares fit in the bottom of the gun.

This gun is the easiest to aim, as far as target practice, and if that's what you'd like it for, I'd recommend this one. I've found it to be a great stress reliever. When the little ones are creating chaos, I can pull out this gun, tape a target to the wall, and do a little target practice.

Twisted Spinner Blaster:

This is the medium sized gun in this line. To shoot it, you pull an arm on the gun back towards yourself. The darts are loaded in the round end. It will hold 8 darts. As with all the guns, it comes with removable shields.

This one is a little harder to aim, but it's still fun.

Rapid Madness Blaster:

This is the largest gun in this line. You push and pull an arm to pump it up. The trigger is super sensitive, so it takes a couple of seconds to shoot all 20 darts that it holds. Those darts are held in a clip that slides into the side of the gun. This one is the most fun, BUT you don't get much shooting time before having to round up darts.

Bandolier:

This is an adjustable strap that you can wear across your body. It has a special target that the darts will stick to. It will also hold 12 extra darts.

Eye goggles:

These are pretty cool. As advertised, they won't fog up. They're made of a thick-like plastic/rubber, and give you "bug vision". They're also adjustable. My little ones are younger than the recommended age, but the clip kept coming off with them, and we put the goggles back together so much that I wanted to throw them away. Still, I don't think adults will have that problem, and they really are pretty cool!

Targets:

These are a little smaller than I prefer, but they do come in slightly different sizes and shapes. You get different points for different areas. The darts DO stick really well to these targets, and ONLY these targets, but if the dart hits wrong, it still won't stick. I'd say our darts stuck about half the time with the larger guns, and about 3/4th of the time with the farshot blaster. You can peel the back off and it will stick to the wall/door, but as I mentioned above, I just taped it instead. They're a fun way to create a little "battle" zone in one's room, or just simple target practice.

Overall, we've had tons of fun with these guns, and just think they're all pretty awesome.
text_fidelity_b: BOOMco. Rapid Madness Blaster (Discontinued by manufacturer)

WOW! Stuff Collection Fantastic Beasts – Newt’s Light Painting Wand – Award Winner! You will open up a huge world of fun with the Wizarding World WW-1024 Harry Potter's Light Painting Wand, Brown. The Harry Potter wand is about 14 inches long with a grainy wood looking black handle and brown wand part that ends with a very bright LED light tip. The wand has a nice feel and weight to it and seems to be made of a strong resin plastic. The wand comes in a lovely window box with directions, customer support information and a bonus app for making your light paintings.

There is a tiny button on the wand’s handle for turning on the LED light which only stays on as long as you hold the button down. The 3 included 1.5 V LR41 batteries are replaceable by opening the handle end with a phillips screwdriver. This is a great thing, as I can see replacing the batteries often, as our kids can’t put this wand down for a minute. For those of you that look forward to some creative light painting, you will want to download the app. Light painting is just photographing a moving light at a longer exposure shutter speed, in the dark, with no flash. You will want the camera on a tripod to get the light design without shaky movement.

In our house, we can’t get the kids to stop playing with the light painting wand long enough for us to try the light painting. Of course we had to buy another wand, as they play Tag with each other in the dark as well as hide and seek in the dark and casting spells on each other- endless fun for them. I just got one of the wands after bedtime to try a bit of light painting. I only used my camera on the Slow Shutter dial, did not have time to set up a tripod, and snapped a couple photos in the dark with no flash. I caught a photo of the wand making a “V”, and it came out nice for no app or tripod yet. I have seen light painting photos that are fantastic when you know how to manually set your camera for long exposures. Adding a colored cellophane over the light tip makes for gorgeous colored lights too. Our kids love playing with these wands and could care less about the light painting for now. These wands are getting a lot of playtime and are a huge hit- especially with Halloween around the corner. 5 STARS.
